facets.facet: Why AI/LLM-Generated UI Drifts into Inconsistency Across Sessions and Components

keyFindings.insight: Context window exhaustion forces re-invention, not hallucination. Models cannot simultaneously load design brief, full component library, all token definitions, AND task instructions. Missing tokens aren't hallucinated; they were never retrievable.
keyFindings.evidence: RAG research (Emulating Retrieval Augmented Generation via Prompt Engineering) confirms models require active retrieval to reference distant code. Hardik Pandya's 'Expose Your Design System to LLMs' explicitly documents that without token indexing, LLMs fabricate values rather than retrieve them. SpecifyUI research shows structured specifications reduce drift by constraining generation space.
keyFindings.implication: A framework cannot rely on 'just include the design system in the prompt.' Context windows will fill with task context first. AI consistency requires RETRIEVAL ARCHITECTURE (indexable token layer, component registry queries, RAG pipeline) not just prompt engineering. The blank-page default exists because retrieval is friction.

keyFindings.insight: Cross-session re-invention is structural to stateless API calls. No memory persists between chat sessions or separate API calls. Button v1 at 11:00 AM (border-radius: 6px) and Button v2 at 2:00 PM (border-radius: 8px) are independent generations with zero mutual awareness.
keyFindings.evidence: Design system adoption research explicitly states LLMs 'lose all context between sessions.' This is not a model flaw—it is architecture. Each API call is a fresh inference with no session state.
keyFindings.implication: Frameworks must implement external state: either persistent component registry (queryable across sessions), post-generation validation against existing patterns, or embedded retrieval that queries 'what exists' before generating. Prompt instruction alone cannot bridge sessions.

keyFindings.insight: Hardcoded literals (12px, #FFFFFF, rgba(0,0,0,0.5)) are not hallucinations—they are cost-optimized outputs. Models emit literals instead of tokens because: (1) tokens weren't in context (retrieval failure), (2) literals are cheaper in tokens to emit, (3) the prompt didn't forbid them. This appears as taste but is mechanism.
keyFindings.evidence: Hardik Pandya research documents the 'tokens.css' three-layer solution (upstream tokens, project aliases, fallbacks) and audit process to identify every hardcoded value (hex, rgb, pixel spacing, font sizes, border radii, z-index, box shadows, transitions). Models drift on values within session when literals are allowed.
keyFindings.implication: System prompts must include hard constraints: 'NEVER emit raw px/color/shadow values. Reference design tokens only.' Token layer indexing (cost ~1K tokens upfront) pays back immediately by eliminating re-discovery. This is mechanical enforcement, not taste judgment.

keyFindings.insight: Sampling variance at temperature > 0 produces measurable value drift (15px vs 16px, #F0F0F0 vs #F5F5F5). Multiple samples of the same prompt yield different numeric outputs. This is not randomness in taste—it is randomness in token selection.
keyFindings.evidence: 'Hot or Cold?' research on adaptive temperature sampling shows code generation requires temperature 0.0–0.3. At temperature 0.5+, error rates climb measurably. Multi-sample aggregation (drawing N samples and voting on the most common output) reduces variance by 13.6% as measured on HumanEval. Most teams use temperature 1.0 for UI code, which is 3–5x higher than optimal.
keyFindings.implication: Frameworks should enforce temperature 0.1–0.3 in generation config, not leave it to users. For critical consistency (token values, color names), use temperature 0.0. Multi-sample aggregation (sample N times, return consensus) is empirically proven; it costs 3x the inference time but eliminates variance drift.

keyFindings.insight: Naming convention ambiguity cascades into divergent component taxonomies. Without explicit naming spec, identical 'build a button' prompts yield Button.tsx, PrimaryButton.tsx, button-primary.tsx in different locations. All are defensible; none are wrong.
keyFindings.evidence: Figma design tokens research shows naming pattern category/role/variant (e.g., color/action/primary) stated explicitly 'eliminates the most persistent friction in design-to-engineering handoff.' Token naming specs from Tokens Studio document that full words, consistent prefixes, and nested hierarchies must be documented in library Docs and codebase README and enforced in reviews.
keyFindings.implication: Naming convention must be explicit constraint in system prompt before generation: 'All components use PascalCase, live in /components, styled with [framework]-specific module pattern.' Without explicit naming, components will be invented with valid but divergent names. This costs zero inference time to specify.

keyFindings.insight: Component inventory blindness means models cannot efficiently query 'what button-like components exist?' without reloading the entire codebase. This produces synonym bloat: Card, CardWrapper, CardComponent, c-card are generated independently, unaware of each other.
keyFindings.evidence: Context window limitations prevent simultaneous loading of large component inventories. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the standard solution: only fetch relevant components when asked to 'build a button'—not all components upfront.
keyFindings.implication: Frameworks should embed a queryable component index (vector search, semantic similarity, or tag-based retrieval) so 'show me similar components' is a low-friction retrieval step before generation. This prevents synonym re-invention.

keyFindings.insight: Taste vs. Retrieval is the key distinction for framework design. A model choosing 12px vs 16px padding is taste (both valid); a model choosing 12px, then later 16px for the same layout without checking is retrieval failure. Treating retrieval failures as taste failures leads to wrong fixes.
keyFindings.evidence: First-principles analysis: taste is a choice from a valid range (not wrong). Retrieval failure is omitting a fact that existed. Research on hallucinations separates token-level variance (measurement via probability signals) from factual errors (API calls that don't exist, functions that weren't defined).
keyFindings.implication: Framework design must separately address: (1) taste (use design tokens, make decisions once at the system level), (2) retrieval (index components, make prior decisions queryable), (3) variance (lower temperature, aggregate samples). Conflating them leads to overengineered prompts that don't fix the real problem.

recommendationsForFramework: Separate RETRIEVAL from GENERATION. Before generating any component, query the component registry (via semantic search or tag-based lookup) to fetch existing similar components. Feed these as reference examples in the context window, not as hidden context. Make the retrieval step explicit in the prompt: 'Found existing Button component at /components/Button.tsx. Use it as reference for styling. If you must create a new variant, name it consistently.'

Enforce a three-layer token architecture: (1) Upstream design tokens (from Figma or design system), (2) Project aliases with semantic names, (3) Fallback values. Index this as a queryable artifact (JSON or CSS variables), not prose. Include the full token index in the system prompt for code generation tasks. Cost: ~1–2K tokens. Benefit: eliminates hardcoded value re-invention.

Add hard constraints to the system prompt: 'NEVER emit raw pixel values, hex colors, or shadow definitions. Reference design tokens only. If a token does not exist, ask for clarification before generating.' Validate generated code against the token layer post-generation.

Set temperature to 0.1–0.2 for UI code generation by default, not 1.0. For critical deterministic outputs (token names, color references), use temperature 0.0. This is low-cost and empirically proven to reduce variance.

Implement multi-sample consensus for high-stakes components: generate the same component 3–5 times with temperature 0.2, then return the most common output (or the one with highest semantic similarity to existing components). Cost: 3–5x inference; benefit: variance drift elimination.

Document and enforce explicit naming conventions in the system prompt before generation. Include format: 'All components use PascalCase filenames, live in /components/[Category]/[Name].tsx, use BEM for CSS classes, export as default.' Link to codebase README that shows examples.

Create a pre-generation retrieval step: before asking the model to 'build a button,' fetch and surface: (1) existing button-like components, (2) naming precedents from the codebase, (3) the token layer for spacing/color/typography. Make these explicit in the prompt: 'Your context includes: [existing components]. Reuse [ComponentName] if it matches your intent.'

Implement a component registry (queryable database or semantic index) that tracks: component name, file path, variant names, tokens used, last modified date, and aliases. Before generation, query for semantic matches ('button-like components'). This is the retrieval bridge across sessions.

Post-generation validation layer: lint generated code for (1) hardcoded values (reject px/color/shadow literals), (2) naming consistency (check against patterns in codebase), (3) token reference validity (check all tokens exist). Flag deviations with high confidence before returning to user.

For cross-session consistency, persist component decisions in a Git-tracked manifest or Figma document that the model can query: 'spacing: {sm: 8px, md: 12px, lg: 16px}, colors: {primary: #0066CC, ...}.' This acts as the single source of truth across sessions.

Use SpecifyUI-style structured specifications (DSL, not natural language) to express design intent before generation. This constrains the generation space and makes intent explicit, reducing variance from ambiguous prompts.
pitfalls: Assuming larger context windows solve re-invention. A 200K-token window still exhausts when you load design system + existing code + instructions. The problem is not window size; it is that retrieval must be active and scoped, not passive inclusion. Expanding windows without fixing retrieval just defers the problem.

Using temperature 0.5–1.0 for UI code and expecting consistency. This introduces measurable variance. Teams often use high temperature for 'creativity,' but UI code has strict syntax rules and visual targets. High temperature produces errors. Many practitioners are unaware of the trade-off; research clearly shows 0.1–0.3 is optimal.

Treating all drift as hallucination. Most UI drift (15px vs 16px, Button vs CardButton) is rational re-invention, not false confidence. Applying hallucination-detection techniques (variance signal analysis, reference-based filters) will not fix retrieval failures. Wrong diagnosis → wrong fix.

Writing comprehensive design system specs in natural language prose and expecting models to follow implicitly. Prose is not queryable; it exhausts context window; it is ambiguous. Models will invent because the spec was not structured as machine-readable constraints.

Assuming naming conventions are 'good practices' and expecting adoption without enforcement. Models will invent unless the system prompt includes explicit naming spec AND post-generation validation rejects deviations. Conventions are enforced, not suggested.

Not distinguishing between multi-session drift and in-session drift. In-session drift (temperature variance, incomplete prompt) has different fixes than cross-session drift (missing external state, no component registry). Treating them the same leads to overengineered prompts that miss the structural problem.

Relying on a single sample per generation. Variance at temperature > 0 is inevitable; the fix is to sample multiple times and aggregate, not to hope a single sample is representative. This costs inference time but is empirically worth it.

Hardcoding token values in the system prompt instead of indexing them. Hard-coded tokens become stale; they exhaust context; they are not discoverable. A queryable token layer (JSON, database, Figma variables) is maintainable and retrievable.

Asking models to 'be consistent' without providing retrieval or external state. Consistency requires memory (not available in stateless API) or retrieval (not enabled by prompts alone). Exhorting the model to 'match existing components' without making prior components queryable is performative.

facets.facet: Design Token Representation & Consumption Across Stacks - Unified Manifest Format for AI-Driven Application

keyFindings.insight: W3C DTCG Specification (2025.10) is the stable, production-ready standard with $value, $type, and $description as core properties. $type is mandatory for type safety and must be explicitly declared (tools MUST NOT guess from value). Types can be inherited from parent groups. Token paths use dot notation (group.token) and support references via curly braces {group.token}.
keyFindings.evidence: [Design Tokens Format Module 2025.10](https://www.designtokens.org/tr/drafts/format/); [W3C announcement Oct 2025](https://www.w3.org/community/design-tokens/2025/10/28/design-tokens-specification-reaches-first-stable-version/)
keyFindings.implication: A unified manifest MUST use $type/$value/$description structure; AI can read token types directly without inference. Type inheritance allows parent group defaults. Curly brace syntax {group.token} is the standard for aliasing—AI can parse this predictably across all platforms.

keyFindings.insight: Token hierarchy has three semantic layers: (1) Primitive tokens (raw, brand-agnostic values like #0066cc, 16px), (2) Semantic tokens (role-based references like {colors.primary} → surface/danger/success), (3) Component tokens (component-specific overrides). Each layer can reference the previous via {group.token} syntax, forming a dependency chain.
keyFindings.evidence: [Contentful Design Tokens Guide](https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/); [Design Good Practices](https://goodpractices.design/articles/design-tokens); [Toolabs Semantic Tokens](https://www.toolabs.com/learn/tokens/semantics/)
keyFindings.implication: Manifest structure should enforce this three-tier hierarchy explicitly: a 'primitive' section (source values), a 'semantic' section (references to primitives), and a 'component' section (component-specific refs). This prevents circular dependencies and makes the intent clear for AI code generation. Aliasing semantic names (not appearance-based) ensures single change propagates everywhere.

keyFindings.insight: Composite tokens are individual tokens with pre-defined sub-value structures (typography, border, shadow, stroke). Distinct from groups: groups are containers outside tokens; composites ARE tokens with object-valued $value. E.g., typography has fontFamily, fontSize, lineHeight, fontWeight as required sub-keys. Border has color, width, style. Shadow is single object or array of shadow objects.
keyFindings.evidence: [DTCG Composite Types](https://deepwiki.com/design-tokens/community-group/3.1.5-composite-types); [Tokens Studio Typography Docs](https://docs.tokens.studio/manage-tokens/token-types/typography/)
keyFindings.implication: Manifest MUST distinguish groups (organizational) from composites (reusable style objects). Composite tokens reduce repetition: a single typography token generates font-family, size, weight, line-height everywhere it's used. AI can recognize composite $type values (typography, border, shadow) and generate multi-property code in a single output.

keyFindings.insight: Style Dictionary (Amazon) is the reference implementation for multi-platform transformation. Core flow: read JSON tokens → apply transforms (name/kebab, color/UIColorSwift, etc.) → output platform-specific code (CSS, Swift, Kotlin, XML). Each platform needs custom transforms and formats. Example: name/kebab converts 'spacing.small' to '--spacing-small' for CSS; name/camel to 'spacingSmall' for JS/TS.
keyFindings.evidence: [Style Dictionary Docs](https://styledictionary.com/getting-started/installation/); [Built-in Formats](https://styledictionary.com/reference/hooks/formats/predefined/)
keyFindings.implication: Manifest should be platform-agnostic; transformation rules are externalized. AI can read ONE manifest and generate build configs (Style Dictionary, Tailwind, custom scripts) that handle all transforms. No need to duplicate token definitions. Transforms are deterministic and versioned.

keyFindings.insight: CSS variables (CSS custom properties) are generated from token names via kebab-case transform. E.g., color.text.primary → --color-text-primary. Tailwind v4 uses @theme directive to define tokens that auto-generate utility classes AND expose as CSS vars at runtime. CSS-first approach collapses token definition and utility generation into single source.
keyFindings.evidence: [Tailwind CSS v4 Blog](https://tailwindcss.com/blog/tailwindcss-v4); [Medium Tailwind v4 Guide](https://medium.com/@sureshdotariya/tailwind-css-4-theme-the-future-of-design-tokens-at-2025-guide-48305a26af06)
keyFindings.implication: For web, manifest can target either CSS vars (lower-level, more control) or Tailwind @theme (higher-level, utilities included). Both read from the same JSON source. AI can detect project setup (pure CSS, Tailwind, other) and emit appropriate output format. CSS vars naming is deterministic: family.name → --family-name.

keyFindings.insight: SwiftUI consumption pattern: tokens → Color extensions + Asset Catalog integration. Xcode 15+ auto-generates static properties (ColorResource) from Asset Catalog. Tokens can be organized as nested enums (DS.Colors, DS.Spacing) or as generated Color extensions from Asset Catalog. Asset Catalog colors support light/dark mode automatically. Generated Swift code uses enum cases mapping to UIColor(named:) or direct Asset Catalog reference.
keyFindings.evidence: [SwiftUI Color Design System Article](https://www.designsystemscollective.com/building-a-swiftui-design-system-part-1-color-2ea75035e691); [Xcode 15 Asset Symbols](https://sarunw.com/posts/swift-symbols-for-asset-catalog/)
keyFindings.implication: iOS output should generate: (1) Swift enum namespace (DS.Colors, DS.Spacing), (2) Color/Font extensions backed by Asset Catalog, (3) Asset Catalog definitions themselves. Token tooling can emit .swift files AND .xcassets definitions. This approach unifies design-time (Asset Catalog UI) and runtime (Swift code) consistency.

keyFindings.insight: Tokens Studio for Figma supports W3C DTCG format natively and can export tokens in standard JSON. Converts between DTCG and legacy formats on demand. Exports 21+ token types to Figma Styles/Variables. This bridges design-to-dev: designers manage tokens in Figma, export DTCG JSON, developers build platform transformations from that single file.
keyFindings.evidence: [Tokens Studio DTCG Format Docs](https://docs.tokens.studio/manage-settings/token-format); [Tokens Studio Export](https://docs.tokens.studio/figma/export/)
keyFindings.implication: Manifest can be sourced from Figma (Tokens Studio export) or maintained separately and imported to Figma. Standard DTCG JSON is the pivot format. AI can read exported JSON from Tokens Studio and apply transforms for all platforms without re-duplicating values.

keyFindings.insight: Token references use {group.token} syntax for value-level aliasing. These resolve to the $value of the target token. Property-level references require JSON Pointer syntax ($ref) and are separate. Circular references are invalid. Resolution is transitive: {primary} can reference {blue-500} can reference an absolute value. Tool MUST validate reference chains during build.
keyFindings.evidence: [DTCG Token References](https://camoa.github.io/dev-guides/design-systems/tailwind-tokens/w3c-design-tokens-format/); [Tokens Studio Token Values](https://docs.tokens.studio/manage-tokens/token-values)
keyFindings.implication: Manifest validation MUST check for circular references before code generation. AI can recursively resolve {ref} chains to emit final values. Reference syntax is unambiguous; parsing is straightforward. Aliasing is single-source: change {primary} once, all dependents update.

keyFindings.insight: Cross-platform transformation requires platform-specific code generators. Android: XML resources + Kotlin code from single JSON source. iOS: Swift code + Asset Catalog from same source. Web: CSS vars + TypeScript enums + Tailwind config from same source. Key insight: one semantic JSON, N code outputs, N build steps (one per platform).
keyFindings.evidence: [Deep Dive on Design Tokens Integration](https://deep-dive-on-design-tokens.com/3-integration/); [Midrocket Cross-Platform Guide](https://midrocket.com/en/guides/design-tokens-guide/)
keyFindings.implication: Manifest is the single source of truth. Code generation is deterministic and version-controlled. CI/CD can regenerate all platform outputs from manifest changes. No manual syncing across platforms. AI reading one manifest can emit code for all targets simultaneously.

keyFindings.insight: Naming conventions are deterministic and toolable. Primitive layer uses raw values (e.g., blue-500, 16px). Semantic layer uses role-based names (color-text-primary, spacing-inset-md). Transforms are stateless: same input token always produces same output name in target language. Kebab-case for CSS, camelCase for JavaScript, snake_case for Python, PascalCase for Swift enums.
keyFindings.evidence: [Design Token Naming Structure](https://medium.com/@brcsndr/you-dont-know-css-design-tokens-naming-structure-52add5d02d82); [Style Dictionary Name Transforms](https://styledictionary.com/reference/hooks/formats/predefined/)
keyFindings.implication: Naming transforms are algorithmic; no human intervention needed. AI can apply predictable transformations to generate platform-specific identifiers. Naming conventions encode semantic meaning (e.g., '-primary' always means 'main/dominant', '-secondary' always means 'supporting') that AI can leverage for context.

keyFindings.insight: Manifest format should minimize duplication. Define values once, reference many times. Composite tokens further reduce duplication: one typography token generates font + size + weight + height. Semantic layer prevents value sprawl: one {primary} aliased 50 times beats 50 hardcoded #0066cc values. This directly supports AI code generation: fewer source lines, more deterministic output.
keyFindings.evidence: [Single Source of Truth in Design Tokens](https://medium.com/dan-stories/design-tokens-the-promise-of-a-single-source-of-truth-cfab82638808); [Contentful Design Token System](https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/)
keyFindings.implication: Manifest structure should penalize duplication and reward abstraction. Tooling should flag un-aliased values (hard-to-maintain). Each token should have clear parent (what does it reference?). This makes AI's job easier: follow the reference chain to understand intent, emit code that preserves that intent.

recommendationsForFramework: Manifest Structure: Define a JSON schema with four top-level sections: (1) 'primitives' (raw, brand-agnostic values with no refs), (2) 'semantic' (role-based tokens referencing primitives via {primitive.token}), (3) 'composite' (typography, border, shadow objects), (4) 'component' (component-specific overrides referencing semantic/composite). Add a 'metadata' section for description, version, author, source-of-truth URL.

Token Definition Rule: Every token MUST have $type, $value, and $description (required). $description should encode semantic intent ('Primary text color across surfaces in default theme', not just 'gray'). AI reads descriptions to infer usage context and validate application correctness.

Reference Syntax: Use DTCG curly-brace syntax {group.token} exclusively for value-level refs. Validate during manifest parsing: detect cycles, resolve transitively, report unresolved refs. Emit a 'resolution map' alongside manifest (token ID → final value, for debugging).

Composite Tokens: Pre-define composite schemas for typography (fontFamily, fontSize, fontWeight, lineHeight, letterSpacing, textDecoration), border (color, width, style), shadow (x, y, blur, spread, color), and transition (duration, easing, delay). Each composite is ONE token, not N separate ones. This prevents fragmentation.

Naming Conventions: Establish layer-based naming: (1) Primitives: raw names like 'blue-500', '16px', 'sans'; (2) Semantic: role-based like 'color-text-primary', 'spacing-inset-lg', 'shadow-elevation-high'; (3) Component: scoped like 'button-primary-background', 'card-border-default'. Document the naming rule in manifest metadata.

Platform Transform Rules: Define per-platform transform chains as data (not code): web → [name/kebab, color/hex, dimension/px] → CSS vars; iOS → [name/camelCase, color/UIColor, dimension/CGFloat] → Swift enum; Android → [name/snake_case, color/hex, dimension/dp] → XML + Kotlin. AI can read these rules and emit code or build configs.

Validation Layer: Manifest parser MUST validate: (1) Every token has $type + $value, (2) All refs {group.token} exist and resolve, (3) No circular refs, (4) Types match expected structure (e.g., typography has required sub-keys), (5) Naming follows declared conventions, (6) Semantic layer only refs primitives/composite, (7) Component layer only refs semantic/composite. Emit validation report.

Source Annotation: Record in every token: $source (where it came from—Figma, Sketch, manual JSON, etc.), $lastUpdated, $owner, $status (stable, experimental, deprecated). AI uses this to warn about stale tokens or propose deletions.

Semantic Layering Enforcement: Make it syntactically obvious that semantic tokens depend on primitives, and component tokens depend on semantic. Manifest parser should reject semantic tokens that ref other semantic tokens (force going through primitives). This prevents implicit layers and circular thinking.

Export + Import Contract: Define a canonical JSON schema (DTCG + extensions for metadata, source). Tools write to this schema; AI reads from this schema. Include a version field (token format version) so tools can adapt when schema evolves. This is the 'contract' between design tools, token tooling, and code generators.

Aliasing Clarity: Document that {ref} does NOT create a new token, it just redirects the value. Multiple tokens can ref the same primitive (e.g., both 'color-text-primary' and 'color-button-text' → {color-blue-900}). This is intentional reuse, not duplication. AI leverages this for impact analysis (change blue-900, here's what updates).

AI-Centric Additions: Add to manifest: (1) 'patterns' section documenting which tokens combine (e.g., button always gets 'color-text-primary' + 'spacing-inset-md' + 'radius-sm'), (2) 'constraints' section (e.g., 'color-text-primary' must have WCAG AAA contrast on color-bg-surface), (3) 'deprecated' section (tokens being phased out with migration guides). AI uses patterns to catch incomplete token applications.
pitfalls: Pitfall: Maintaining multiple token sources (Figma, Tokens Studio, manual JSON, Tailwind config). AI reads the wrong file or outdated copy. Reality: Even with Figma as source-of-truth, exports lag, and developers often have local overrides. Solution requires a clear 'canonical manifest' location and a CI pipeline that re-generates and validates all outputs from it.

Pitfall: Over-naming—creating 'token layers' that are really just renamed copies of the same value (e.g., color-primary, color-button-primary, button-bg all = #0066cc). Defeats semantic meaning and creates aliasing confusion. Solution: Force explicit refs {primitive}; disallow duplicate values without a documented reason (e.g., 'intentional exception for dark mode variant').

Pitfall: Assuming transform rules are universal. Reality: CSS vars work in all browsers, but Tailwind v4 @theme only works with Tailwind. SwiftUI Asset Catalog integration requires Xcode 15+. Android XML differs from Compose. AI must detect platform version/constraints before applying transforms.

Pitfall: Composites that are actually 'style presets' (e.g., 'card' = padding + radius + shadow + background). These should be generated component definitions, not tokens. Tokens are primitive building blocks; composites are predefined combinations. Conflating them leads to uncomposabl code (can't use half a card).

Pitfall: Token descriptions that repeat the name ('primary button primary color') instead of explaining intent ('main brand color for interactive elements; ensures sufficient contrast on light backgrounds'). AI can't infer usage from tautological descriptions. Solution: Require descriptions to answer 'why' and 'where', not just 'what'.

Pitfall: Unversioned transformations. A tool generates output based on current transform rules, then months later the rules change silently. Output from month 1 no longer matches month 3 rules. Solution: Version transform rules explicitly; include rule version in generated code as a comment. AI can warn about mismatches.

Pitfall: Not validating reference chains at token-definition time. Circular refs, dead refs, type mismatches discovered only at code-generation time (or worse, at runtime). Solution: Eager validation during manifest parsing; error before any code is generated.

Pitfall: Ignoring that semantic naming requires design intent, not just technical consistency. Two 'primary' tokens with different constraints (e.g., one for light theme only, one for both) masquerade as the same thing. Solution: Use variant qualifiers {primary-light}, {primary-dark} or explicit theme keys, not overloaded semantic names.

Pitfall: Assuming CSS vars alone solve cross-platform consistency. Reality: CSS vars only work in browsers; they don't generate Swift enums or Kotlin code. Even within web, CSS vars don't generate TypeScript types (you still need a separate TS enum or type). Solution: Token is source; CSS vars are one output; TypeScript types are another output. Don't conflate them.

Pitfall: Overlooking composite token sub-value types. A shadow token can have its color reference a primitive color token. If the primitive changes, the composite updates. But if the shadow is used directly without referencing sub-tokens, it's fragile. Solution: Require composite sub-values to be token refs, not hardcoded (shadow.color: {primitive-color} not shadow.color: #000).

facets.facet: Infrastructure for Reliable Component Reuse in Code Generators: Registry Models, Design-to-Code Bridges, and Agent-Discoverable Metadata

keyFindings.insight: shadcn/ui Registry Model uses a two-level schema: registry.json (catalog index) and registry-item.json (individual component metadata). Each item requires name, type, and optionally title, description, dependencies, files array, cssVars, and a custom 'meta' object for arbitrary key-value pairs.
keyFindings.evidence: shadcn/ui official documentation (registry-item-json spec) confirms required fields: $schema, name, type; optional: title, description, author, dependencies, devDependencies, registryDependencies, files (with path/type/target), cssVars, docs, categories, meta object
keyFindings.implication: Registry items lack explicit 'when-to-use' and 'anti-patterns' fields by design—they rely on external documentation (docs field points to markdown) rather than machine-readable intent. This requires agents to fetch and parse separate docs rather than making decisions from structured metadata alone.

keyFindings.insight: Figma Code Connect creates bidirectional mapping between design components and code components using template files (.figma.tsx, .figma.jsx, etc.) that export an object with three critical fields: example (code snippet), imports (required libraries), and id (unique identifier). The mapping is anchored by a URL comment linking to the Figma component node.
keyFindings.evidence: Figma Code Connect quickstart and CLI docs specify that templates export { example, imports, id } and use figma.config.json to define label, language, and file include patterns. Methods like getString(), getBoolean(), getEnum() extract component properties.
keyFindings.implication: Code Connect provides visibility into what code implementations exist for a design component, but the mapping is unidirectional from design→code intent. It doesn't expose component relationships, variants as structured data, or anti-patterns—it primarily shows 'here is the code snippet for this design node,' not 'when to use this vs. alternatives.'

keyFindings.insight: Custom Elements Manifest (CEM) standardizes metadata for web components with fields: schemaVersion, modules (with kind, name, tagName, description, members[], events[], attributes[], superclass), and exports. It enables IDE support, documentation generation, and framework integration but is primarily structural/API metadata, not semantic usage guidance.
keyFindings.evidence: Custom Elements Manifest spec (schema v2.1.0) published at github.com/webcomponents/custom-elements-manifest; designed for tooling integration and component discovery but lacks 'purpose', 'when-to-use', or 'incompatible-with' fields
keyFindings.implication: CEM excels at exposing what a component can do (its API surface) but not why an agent should reach for it over alternatives. It's a structural contract, not a semantic one.

keyFindings.insight: Storybook Component Manifest automatically generates JSON metadata from CSF files and source code analysis, exposing: id, name, path, description, import, stories (with id/name/snippet), jsDocTags, and reactDocgen (including props with required, tsType, description, defaultValue). The manifest is framework-agnostic but currently unstable (not a public API).
keyFindings.evidence: Storybook official docs (ai/manifests) show manifest structure accessed at /manifests/components.json; generated from static CSF analysis and prop extraction. Includes stories array with usage snippets and JSDoc metadata.
keyFindings.implication: Storybook provides usage examples (story snippets) and type information, but lacks explicit 'anti-patterns', 'component relationships', or 'when-to-use' fields. Agents get 'here's how to use it' but not 'don't use it like this' or 'use Button instead of Link for actions.'

keyFindings.insight: Agentic Design System best practices require three additional metadata layers beyond API/variant specs: (1) Relationships (parent containers, common locations, incompatible neighbors), (2) Anti-patterns (product-specific usage rules like 'never destructive button in onboarding', 'two primary buttons never side-by-side'), and (3) Purpose statement (explicit semantic intent, not just variant names).
keyFindings.evidence: TDP blog 'Agentic Design System' and Romina Kavcic's 'Ultimate AI Component Generation' framework identify 16 fields; anti-patterns described as 'the most under-rated metadata element' with empirical reduction in generation failures from 40% to 5% when explicit metadata provided
keyFindings.implication: Structured anti-patterns metadata is the critical differentiator between AI agents that generate reusable components vs. those that generate novel (broken) ones. Current registries (shadcn, CEM, Storybook) don't standardize anti-patterns fields.

keyFindings.insight: MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers for design systems expose component catalogs with metadata about capabilities, authentication, input/output specs. Storybook MCP server and design system MCP servers consume component manifests and present them in an LLM-optimized payload, enabling agents to discover and reason about components without full context.
keyFindings.evidence: Storybook MCP sneak peek and Design Systems MCP RFC (github.com/storybookjs/ds-mcp-experiment-reshaped) show MCP as the abstraction layer. MCP registries track metadata around capabilities, endpoints, and authentication; truefoundry.com/blog/best-mcp-registries documents metadata surface.
keyFindings.implication: MCP is the runtime discovery and connection layer, but the metadata quality (anti-patterns, relationships, intent) is still delegated to upstream registries. MCP acts as a broker, not a schema enforcer.

keyFindings.insight: No current system (shadcn, Code Connect, CEM, Storybook, MCP) standardizes these critical fields: (a) semantic intent/purpose statement, (b) when-to-use heuristics, (c) incompatibilities (which components should never coexist), (d) variant interaction rules (e.g., 'disabled state incompatible with loading state'), (e) accessibility constraints, (f) responsive behavior rules, (g) design token requirements per variant.
keyFindings.evidence: Cross-reference of all five systems shows: shadcn lacks 'anti-patterns' field (relies on external docs); Code Connect lacks variant metadata; CEM lacks semantic intent; Storybook lacks anti-patterns and relationships; MCP is only a transport layer
keyFindings.implication: Agents must infer component usage patterns from free-form documentation, stories, or examples rather than structured, machine-queryable metadata. This is the root cause of AI systems generating novel components instead of reusing existing ones.

keyFindings.insight: Minimal metadata set required for agent-reliable component reuse: (1) Canonical Name & ID, (2) Purpose Statement (intent, not just label), (3) Props Schema (types, required, defaults), (4) Variants Map (all state/size/style combinations), (5) Anti-Patterns Array (explicit don'ts), (6) Relationships (parent context, incompatible neighbors), (7) Import Path, (8) When-to-Use Heuristics, (9) Accessibility Requirements, (10) Design Tokens Required.
keyFindings.evidence: Synthesis of agentic design system best practices + Kavcic's 16-field framework + empirical reduction in generation errors when metadata provided; no single existing system provides all 10 fields
keyFindings.implication: A custom component manifest schema is necessary if the goal is reliable reuse. Existing systems are each missing 60-70% of what agents need.

recommendationsForFramework: Define a unified component manifest schema that extends (not replaces) shadcn's registry-item format: add top-level fields for purposeStatement, antiPatterns, relationships, whenToUse, and accessibilityRequirements. This can coexist with shadcn's existing meta object for backward compatibility.

Embed usage examples as structured data (not prose): include a usageScenarios array with fields { scenario, code, preferredComponent, whyNotAlternative } so agents can pattern-match on intent rather than guessing from story snippets.

Explicitly codify anti-patterns as a schema: antiPatterns should be an array of { pattern, reason, correctAlternative, severity }. Severity levels (must-not, should-not, deprecated) allow agents to trade off urgency. Include product-specific rules (e.g., 'onboarding flow' → 'disable destructive variants').

Define component relationships as a graph: relationships field should specify parentContexts (container types where valid), incompatibleWith (other component IDs), requiredNeighbors, and optionalNeighbors. This enables agents to validate placement and prevent isolated-component reuse.

Create a variant interaction matrix: variantCombinations should define which prop values can coexist. Example: { disabled: true, loading: true } is invalid. This prevents agents from generating nonsensical state combinations.

Map design tokens as required fields per variant: tokenMap should link each variant to its design tokens (color, spacing, typography) with fallback values. Agents then know 'if I use the secondary variant, I must include these 3 tokens.'

Add accessibility as structured constraints: a11y field should list ARIA attributes, keyboard interactions, semantic HTML requirements, and focus management rules—not as prose documentation but as a queryable schema { attribute, value, required, variants }.

Include responsive and interaction rules: rules field (array) captures 'mobile: stack vertically', 'touch: 44px minimum', 'animation: 150ms ease-in-out', 'keyboard: arrow keys cycle through options'. This prevents responsive/motion mistakes.

Wire manifests into MCP servers: create a standard MCP interface (list_components, get_component_metadata, search_by_purpose, find_alternatives) that normalizes across shadcn registries, Storybook manifests, Code Connect mappings, and custom systems. MCP becomes the discovery layer, not just transport.

Version and validate manifests: add manifestVersion and a JSON Schema validator so agents can reject incomplete or malformed component metadata early. Define minimum required fields (canonical-name, purposeStatement, variants, antiPatterns) and optional enrichments (relationships, tokens, a11y).

Provide component relationship reasoning: expose a reasoning field where humans explain why component A is the right choice over B (e.g., 'Use Button for actions, Link for navigation; Button has built-in loading states, Link does not'). Agents use this to inform decisions.

Export as LLM-optimized summaries: generate a human-readable component card (markdown or JSON) that agents can include in prompt context: name, purpose, when-to-use, anti-patterns, variants, imports, a single good example. This is cheaper than loading full metadata for every component lookup.
pitfalls: Treating variant documentation as sufficient: Stories and examples show how to use variants, but don't tell agents when NOT to combine them. A component can have (size, color, disabled, loading) variants individually, but (disabled=true, loading=true) is nonsensical. Free-form docs won't catch this; agents need explicit variant interaction rules.

Over-relying on import paths for discoverability: Agents may find the import path but not know why they should reach for this component vs. a simpler alternative. Purpose and anti-patterns metadata are more important than import clarity for driving reuse.

Assuming type information (TypeScript props) is equivalent to usage guidance: A prop like 'variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary'' is syntactically correct but semantically empty. Agents need to know 'primary is for important actions, secondary for supporting actions; never use primary for confirmation dialogs' — this can't be inferred from the type signature.

Storing anti-patterns in free-form documentation: 'Check the README for usage guidelines' puts the burden on agents to parse natural language. If anti-patterns are buried in prose, agents will miss them or misinterpret them. Anti-patterns must be structured and indexed.

Forgetting product-specific context: Generic anti-patterns (e.g., 'don't disable a button without a reason') are obvious and less useful. The valuable anti-patterns are product-specific: 'never use destructive button in onboarding', 'secondary buttons must have text labels, not icons', 'dropdowns can't appear in top nav below 768px'. These won't be in generic registries; they must be injected as project-level overrides.

Assuming one component per use case: A design system may have Button, IconButton, and Link. An agent needs to know which one fits the current context (navigation, action, toggle). If the manifest doesn't explicitly state 'use Link for navigation, Button for actions', agents will guess and generate novel components instead of reusing existing ones.

Neglecting responsive and interaction rules: A component may be valid at desktop but invalid at mobile (e.g., dropdown vs. modal, horizontal slider vs. vertical). Without explicit rules (breakpoints, gesture handlers, animation timing), agents generate breakpoint-unaware components that fail in production.

Storing metadata in design tools only (Figma Code Connect): Design-side metadata is useful for designers but unreachable from code-generation tools. If the single source of truth is in Figma, agents need Code Connect or Figma MCP access; if it's in code (registry.json, custom manifest), designers can't sync back. Metadata must live in code (source of truth for agents) with tooling to sync back to design.

Using unstable or framework-specific schemas: Storybook manifests are explicitly 'not a public API' as of now. Building agent logic around unstable schemas locks you into breaking changes. Define your own schema, versioned and validated, even if it mirrors existing systems.

Conflating API documentation with reuse guidance: Prop types, JSDoc, TypeScript definitions are necessary but not sufficient. A component can be 'correct' (types are valid) but 'wrong' (chosen for the wrong reason). Agents need semantic guidance, not just syntactic validation.

facets.facet: Design Consistency Measurement Framework: Composite Scoring from Generated Code

keyFindings.insight: Token-Adherence Score measures what fraction of all styled values reference defined design tokens vs. raw literals. Computation: Parse CSS/React/SwiftUI AST to find all declarations with values (colors, spacings, font-sizes, radii). Count references to token variables (e.g., 'var(--color-primary)', 'DS.Spacing.md', 'Color.dsSurface'). Formula: token-adherence = (token_references / all_styled_declarations) * 100. Denominator includes ALL declarations where a token *could* be used (padding, margin, font-size, color, border-radius, line-height, font-weight, box-shadow, etc.). Excludes 'auto', '0', 'inherit', 'current', unitless numbers like 'z-index' values. Raw pixels/ems/rems that don't match any defined token count as numerator-0.
keyFindings.evidence: Project Wallace CSS metrics tool groups unique colors/font-sizes to show consistency. stylelint-declaration-strict-value enforces token usage. Atlassian/MetaMask ESLint plugins (via GitHub) enforce design token usage in TypeScript/JavaScript. Design System Metrics Collection (thedesignsystem.guide) defines 'consistency score = % of screens built entirely with approved tokens'.
keyFindings.implication: This metric is the most direct measure of design system compliance and token penetration. High score (>85%) indicates code generation respects token constraints. Implementable via AST parsing (Babel for React, @swiftast or swiftsyntax for SwiftUI) and CSS parsing (postcss, lightningcss).

keyFindings.insight: Component-Reuse Score captures what fraction of UI instances reuse existing components vs. creating new ones. Computation: (1) Identify all component instances in codebase via AST. For React: count JSX element references matching defined component library names. For SwiftUI: count View instances calling pre-defined struct/modifier names. (2) For each component instance, check if it reuses an existing component definition (black-box reuse) vs. inline styling/new props (variation reuse). (3) Separately count 'missed reuse opportunities' via clone detection (compare DOM trees or View hierarchies; flag when 3+ instances have near-identical structure <15% AST edit distance). Formula: component_reuse = (reused_instances + variation_reuses) / (total_instances + missed_opportunities). Range 0–100%.
keyFindings.evidence: Academic literature (Poulin's RCR metric, arxiv.org/pdf/1406.3727) defines reuse ratio. SourceMeter counts component/class reuses via import analysis. Code clone detection (arxiv 2502.04073) uses metrics from confusion matrices. Research shows reuse rate as ground truth for reusability assessment (ScienceDirect 2019).
keyFindings.implication: Measures whether LLM-generated code leverages existing component library or reinvents. Implementable via AST dependency graph traversal + dynamic call graph analysis. Requires baseline inventory of 'approved' components in manifest.

keyFindings.insight: Value-Clustering Score measures design consistency by counting distinct values in each design dimension (heights, colors, spacings, border-radii, font-sizes). Lower count = higher consistency. Computation: (1) Extract all CSS declarations and parsed style attributes. (2) For each dimension (padding/margin → spacings; color/background → colors; border-radius → radii; font-size → typography; line-height → leading), extract unique VALUES (e.g., '16px', '#FF0000', 'bold'). Treat '16px' and '1rem' as different unless normalized. (3) Count unique values per dimension. (4) Compute clustering_efficiency = 1 - (unique_values_observed / expected_values_if_token_scale_used). For a 5-token spacing scale, if code uses 12 distinct spacing values, efficiency = 1 - (12/5) clamped to [0,1] or score as 5/12 = 41.7%. (5) Aggregate across dimensions with weighted average (colors 30%, spacings 30%, typography 20%, radii 10%, shadows 10%).
keyFindings.evidence: Project Wallace extracts unique colors and font-sizes; CSS Stats (cssstats.com) reports count of distinct colors, font-families, font-sizes. TokenLens (tokenlens.app) analyzes distinct token values vs. definitions. Sparkbox Design System Maturity Model emphasizes 'reduced unique values' as consistency marker.
keyFindings.implication: Direct quantitative proxy for visual coherence. Easy to compute from parsed CSS/AST. High clustering (few distinct values) correlates with design system maturity.

keyFindings.insight: Cross-Session Convergence Score measures agreement between independent LLM agents on the same task. Given N independent runs of code generation on identical prompt, compute inter-rater reliability. (1) Normalize generated code (variable names, whitespace, formatting). (2) Compute pairwise AST edit distance (tree-edit distance / max tree size). (3) For each pair of runs, extract styled values (colors, spacings, sizes). (4) Measure agreement: % of value selections where N runs agreed on the *same token* or *same raw value*. (5) Compute Cohen's Kappa or Krippendorff's Alpha across runs: alpha = (observed_agreement - expected_random_agreement) / (1 - expected_random_agreement). (6) Scale to 0–100%. Minimum 3 independent runs recommended.
keyFindings.evidence: Research (arxiv 2506.12376, 2412.00543, 2505.21999) uses Krippendorff's Alpha and Cohen's Kappa for LLM consistency. Structural entropy metric (arxiv 2508.14288) measures generation stability. UI issue detection study (arxiv 2512.04262) reports Cohen's Kappa 0.50 (moderate) for cross-session agreement.
keyFindings.implication: Measures reliability of LLM design generation. High convergence (>0.70 alpha) = deterministic, replicable outputs. Low convergence (<0.50) = model struggles with consistency. Requires running generation multiple times; not a single-pass metric.

keyFindings.insight: Composite Design Consistency Score = weighted combination of the four sub-metrics. Proposed weights: token_adherence(40%) + component_reuse(30%) + value_clustering(20%) + cross_session_convergence(10%). Each sub-metric normalized to 0–100 scale. Composite = (0.40 × token_adherence) + (0.30 × component_reuse) + (0.20 × clustering_efficiency × 100) + (0.10 × convergence_alpha × 100). Result is single 0–100% score. Interpretation: 0–50 = poor (heavy token violations, frequent reinvention, high value scatter, low convergence); 50–75 = developing (partial token use, some reuse, moderate clustering, moderate agreement); 75–90 = mature (strong token adherence, high component reuse, tight clustering, high convergence); 90–100 = excellent (comprehensive token coverage, maximal reuse, minimal distinct values, excellent cross-session agreement).
keyFindings.evidence: Design System Maturity Model (Sparkbox, Catriona Shedd) uses multi-dimensional scoring. Number Analytics Design System Maturity framework scores on governance, adoption, quality. Netguru's 'How to Master Design System Metrics' advocates multi-layered evaluation. Figma blog 'design-systems-104-making-metrics-matter' endorses blended quantitative + qualitative assessment.
keyFindings.implication: Single composite number for tracking design consistency over time and comparing across generated outputs. Weights can be tuned per organization (e.g., prioritize token_adherence if design system is critical; prioritize convergence if LLM reliability is uncertain).

keyFindings.insight: Implementation Toolchain: (A) CSS/React: Use Babel (@babel/parser) to parse JSX, extract styled declarations. Use postcss or lightningcss to parse CSS. Compare values against manifest of approved tokens (JSON file). (B) SwiftUI: Use SwiftSyntax (Swift package) or swift-ast (GitHub) to parse Swift AST. Walk AST for ViewModifier applications, property assignments. Normalize whitespace and format before AST comparison. (C) Manifest: Design system JSON file listing all approved tokens: {spacings: {xs: '4px', ...}, colors: {primary: '#1F77B4', ...}, typographies: {...}}. (D) Clone detection: Implement tree-edit-distance or use existing tool (e.g., Tree-Sitter, Simian). (E) Statistical aggregation: Pandas/NumPy for cross-session stats; compute Krippendorff's Alpha via krippendorff library (Python) or custom implementation.
keyFindings.evidence: Babel/postcss are standard for code analysis. SwiftSyntax is official Apple library. Tree-Sitter (GitHub tree-sitter) is widely used for clone detection. Krippendorff's Alpha is standard statistical measure for inter-rater reliability (cited in arxiv papers on LLM consistency).
keyFindings.implication: Framework is technically achievable with standard tools. No proprietary dependencies required. Can be integrated into CI/CD pipeline to compute score on every generation run.

recommendationsForFramework: Establish a Design System Manifest as single source of truth before scoring. Define approved tokens for spacing (xs, sm, md, lg, xl with exact pixel values), colors (semantic names + hex codes), typography (font-family, size, weight, line-height), border-radii, shadows. Without this, token-adherence and clustering scores are meaningless.

Define token-adherence exclusions explicitly: decide whether 'auto', '0', 'inherit', unitless numbers (z-index), and vendor prefixes count as violations or are exempted. Document this in a validation ruleset.

For component-reuse, maintain a canonical component library inventory with hash/fingerprint of each component's structure. Use this to detect when generated code creates near-duplicates of existing components (>85% structural similarity).

Normalize CSS values before comparison: convert '#FF0000', 'rgb(255,0,0)', and 'red' to a canonical representation (e.g., hex lowercase) so string-equality doesn't penalize semantic equivalence. SwiftUI: normalize Color extensions similarly.

For value-clustering, choose a baseline: what is the 'expected' number of distinct values if tokens were perfectly adopted? E.g., if you define 5 spacing tokens, efficiency = min(unique_values, 5) / 5. This provides a principled denominator.

Cross-session convergence requires at least 3 independent generation runs. Recommend 5+ for statistical confidence. Set a threshold: runs below 0.60 Krippendorff's Alpha should trigger manual review (LLM output too non-deterministic).

Composite weighting (40/30/20/10) is a starting point. Tune based on project priority: token-heavy design system → raise token_adherence weight to 50–60%. LLM reliability critical → raise convergence to 20–25%. Document weight rationale.

Report sub-scores separately, not just composite. Developers need to know where they're losing points: 'token-adherence 65% (many hardcoded spacings), component-reuse 78% (some missed duplication), clustering 82% (14 font-sizes vs. 7 defined).'

Track scores longitudinally (per sprint, per release). Plot all four sub-metrics on a dashboard. Early detection of drift: if token-adherence drops 5%+ between runs, flag the generation prompts or fine-tune criteria.

Automate scoring in CI: compute on every generation run and fail gates if composite score < threshold (e.g., require >75% before code review). Provide remediation hints (e.g., 'replace hardcoded padding(16) with DS.Spacing.md').

Validate against human code review: correlate automated scores with design/eng team feedback. If high score but poor UX feedback, adjust weighting or exclusion rules. Scores should explain team opinion, not replace it.

Establish tiers for different platforms: React web may have different token scope/density than SwiftUI mobile. Define separate manifests and weight adjustments per platform if multi-platform generation is in scope.
Document all metric definitions in a single specification document (e.g., 'design-consistency-metrics-v1.md') co-owned by design and engineering. Version it; breaking changes require agreement.
pitfalls: Token-adherence ignores semantic correctness: high score if values reference *any* token, even wrong ones. E.g., using DS.Spacing.md (16px) for a color value would technically 'pass' token-adherence check if not caught. Mitigate: add type-checking layer (color declarations must reference color tokens, not spacing tokens).

Component-reuse penalty for intentional variants: a generated component that deliberately diverges from a library component (e.g., a larger button variant) will be flagged as reinvention. Mitigate: distinguish reuse (same definition) from variation (same base + explicit overrides); only penalize the latter if overrides bypass style protocol/enum.

Value-clustering penalizes responsive design: CSS with media queries naturally generates distinct values (16px on mobile, 24px on desktop). Raw distinct-value count will be high even if values are intentional. Mitigate: cluster by *intent* (group all 'body text sizes' together) or strip media queries for clustering analysis.

Cross-session convergence is only 10% of score: two runs producing beautiful, highly reusable code that differ only in naming or formatting would score 90/100 on other metrics but fail convergence if not normalized first. Mitigate: aggressive whitespace/variable-name normalization before AST comparison.

Composite weighting hides component failures: a 75% composite score masks: 90% token-adherence but 45% component-reuse. Non-obvious from single number. Mitigate: visualize radar chart of all four sub-metrics; flag if any sub-score is <60%.

Manifest drift: if design system manifest is not kept in sync with actual approved tokens, token-adherence score becomes meaningless. Old values in manifest cause false positives; missing new tokens cause false negatives. Mitigate: version control manifest; auto-update from design tool (Figma tokens plugin → JSON export).

False reuse detection via string matching: if two components happen to have the same textual naming but different intended behavior, clone detection may incorrectly flag them as reusable. Mitigate: use semantic similarity (behavior + prop signature) not just syntax.

Frozen weights ignore evolution: weights (40/30/20/10) assumed all metrics equally useful. Early-stage systems may need high token_adherence; mature systems may prioritize convergence. Mitigate: review and adjust weights quarterly based on cohort feedback.

Threshold overconfidence: declaring '75% = mature' assumes all organizations have equivalent maturity targets. A startup may be satisfied at 60%; a large enterprise at 90%. Mitigate: define tier expectations per organization, not universal.

AST normalization bugs: different formatting/dialects produce different AST hashes. React: '16px' vs '16 px' vs 'calc(8px + 8px)' will differ. SwiftUI: 'padding(16)' vs '.padding(16)' vs 'padding(.md)'. Mitigate: aggressive canonicalization layer before comparison.

Missing metrics for visual fidelity: high design consistency score does NOT guarantee visually correct UI. Pixel-perfect accuracy requires visual regression testing or human review. Mitigate: design consistency is a necessary but not sufficient condition; supplement with screenshot diffing.

N runs for convergence too expensive: computing 5 independent generation runs x deployment frequency = high LLM API cost. Mitigate: sample convergence on 1-2 sprints/month, not every commit; accept higher variance on individual runs.

facets.facet: SwiftUI Design Consistency: Native Enforcement Points, JSON→Swift Codegen, and Drift Detection via Static Analysis

keyFindings.insight: @Entry macro (Swift 5.9+, Xcode 16+) eliminates boilerplate for custom EnvironmentValues—makes environment-cascading tokens the ergonomic path. Strongly enforces semantic design values over free parameters.
keyFindings.evidence: avanderlee.com (@Entry macro: Creating custom environment values in SwiftUI), donnywals.com (Adding values to the SwiftUI environment with @Entry), hackingwithswift.com. Macro generates EnvironmentKey conformance + EnvironmentValues extension automatically, reducing token-per-value from ~15 lines of boilerplate to a single @Entry line with default value.
keyFindings.implication: v1 framework should promote @Entry for scalar tokens (colors, spacing, density, theme) that cascade. Enables single-point theme injection and cascading semantic values across entire view tree. Drift signal: raw EnvironmentKey code without @Entry suggests older pattern; v2 should suggest migration to macros.

keyFindings.insight: Custom Layout protocol + Subview.spacing(_:) API enforce spacing rules structurally. Layout.sizeThatFits() and Layout.placeSubviews() separate measurement from positioning, making layout-constant drift detectable.
keyFindings.evidence: swiftui-fieldguide.com (Layout protocol), swiftwithmajid.com (Building custom layout spacing), hackingwithswift.com (Custom Layout protocol). Subview proxy exposes spacing(from:) to query platform-oriented spacing preferences; custom layouts that override must document their reasoning.
keyFindings.implication: v2 should support defining custom layouts (e.g., DSSpacingVStack) that accept only enum-based spacing (not CGFloat), making raw-literal padding/spacing detectable as drift. Layout is most ergonomic for enforcing consistent grid/flow. Lint signal: custom Layout without spacing validation.

keyFindings.insight: ShapeStyle protocol + Color extension conformance allow design tokens to work everywhere foregroundStyle(), fill(), stroke() are used—tokens become first-class modifiers, not workarounds.
keyFindings.evidence: swift.mackarous.com (SwiftUI Modifiers Deep Dive: foregroundStyle), magnuskahr.dk (Design System Considerations: Semantic Colors), freiwald.dev (Custom ShapeStyle for SwiftUI Theming). Extensions on ShapeStyle where Self == Color enable tokens like .foregroundStyle(.dsTextPrimary) without casting.
keyFindings.implication: v2 should prefer ShapeStyle-based color tokens over loose Color extensions. Enables semantic color tokens to work in all style contexts. Drift signal: direct Color.red or Color(hex:) usage instead of semantic ShapeStyle extension; .foregroundStyle without semantic namespace suggests hardcoded color.

keyFindings.insight: Asset Catalog color sets (Appearances: Any, Dark) provide native dark-mode and theming support. One Color("name") call resolves light/dark automatically—this is the single most ergonomic enforcement point for semantic colors.
keyFindings.evidence: apple.com (Asset Catalogs + Dark Mode), samwize.com (Asset Catalog and Dark Mode), medium.com/@garejakirit (Best Practices for Organizing Colors). Define ColorSet in Xcode with light/dark variants; SwiftUI's Color initializer queries Asset Catalog at runtime and selects correct variant.
keyFindings.implication: v1 framework should mandate Asset Catalog color sets as single source of truth. v2 scorer should flag Color(red:green:blue:) and hex initializers as drift. Dark-mode compliance becomes automatic if all colors use Asset Catalog; detecting drift via grep for raw RGB calls is high-signal.

keyFindings.insight: ButtonStyle, ToggleStyle, LabelStyle, PickerStyle protocols are the correct native home for component variants. Variants-as-enums (not free parameters) prevent ad-hoc sizing/padding and make reuse ergonomic.
keyFindings.evidence: hackingwithswift.com (Customizing Button with ButtonStyle), avanderlee.com (SwiftUI Button: Custom Styles), swiftui-lab.com (Custom Styling). Each style protocol provides a Configuration type exposing label/toggle state; enum-variant pattern structurally prevents parameterized styling.
keyFindings.implication: v1 framework should model variants as enums (DSButtonStyle.Variant { case primary, secondary, danger }). v2 scorer flags ButtonStyle definitions that accept free parameters (size, padding, radius) as anti-patterns. Drift signal: modifier chains applied directly to Button without a Style protocol wrapper.

keyFindings.insight: SwiftGen, SwiftTokenGen, and Style Dictionary enable JSON→Swift codegen. Style Dictionary transforms JSON tokens into Swift enums; SwiftTokenGen handles Figma + Amazon Style Dictionary exports directly. Macro-based codegen (like @Entry) avoids string-based APIs.
keyFindings.evidence: github.com/SwiftGen (SwiftGen: code generator for assets), github.com/chrishoste/SwiftTokenGen, styledictionary.com (Style Dictionary), swiftforjs.dev (Using style-dictionary), designsystemscollective.com (Tokens to Code Chapter 2). Style Dictionary config specifies JSON source, transformers, and output platform (iOS Swift).
keyFindings.implication: v2 should define design-system.json using DTCG (Design Token Community Group) or Amazon Style Dictionary format. Build step runs codegen (e.g., SwiftTokenGen) to produce DS.swift enum from tokens. Enables single source of truth across platforms. Manifest can be auto-generated from JSON codegen output. Drift signal: manually-typed DS values that diverge from JSON source.

keyFindings.insight: SwiftLint's no_magic_numbers rule detects numeric literals including color hex and RGB; custom_rules enable regex patterns to ban specific usages (Color.red, padding(16), frame(height: 48)). Lint rules are the enforcement layer for scoring—they turn design system rules into CI/editor feedback.
keyFindings.evidence: realm.github.io/SwiftLint (no_magic_numbers rule, custom_rules), github.com/realm/SwiftLint. no_magic_numbers catches #colorLiteral(red:green:blue:alpha:) and numeric constants; custom_rules accept regex patterns targeting specific names (e.g., 'Color\.red|Color\.blue').
keyFindings.implication: v2 scorer should integrate SwiftLint custom_rules configuration to detect: (1) padding/frame/cornerRadius with numeric literals; (2) Color.red, Color.blue (system colors); (3) inline .font(.system(size:)); (4) raw UIColor/CGFloat initializers. Scoring combines lint violations + grep patterns. CI should fail on violations.

keyFindings.insight: Grep patterns for static drift detection: \bpadding\((\d+)\), \bframe\(height:\s*(\d+)\), \bcornerRadius\((\d+)\), Color\.(red|blue|green), \bfont\(.*\.system\(size:. These catch bare numeric tokens and system color abuse. AST analysis via SourceKit enables data-flow tracking for unregistered tokens.
keyFindings.evidence: hackingwithswift.com (Swift Regex 5.7+), github.com/realm/SwiftLint (custom_rules regex syntax), designsystemscollective.com. Swift 5.7+ Regex literals (/pattern/) enable readable pattern matching; AST via SourceKit (used by SwiftLint + sourcekit-lsp) enables symbol resolution and constant tracing.
keyFindings.implication: v2 scorer baseline should include curated grep patterns to detect drift signals: bare spacing/sizing literals, system colors, inline font definitions. Advanced scorer (v3) could parse AST to detect constants used outside DS namespace and trace unregistered values. Patterns should be configurable (whitelist/blacklist by token category).

keyFindings.insight: Environment + @Entry + custom EnvironmentKey macros are the strongest enforcement point for cascading design values (theme, density, accessibility settings). When a value is Environment-backed, it becomes nearly impossible to override locally without refactoring; this makes it ergonomic to enforce.
keyFindings.evidence: swiftwithvincent.com (Using a Swift macro to generate EnvironmentKey), michaellong.medium.com (Debugging SwiftUI's Entry Macro), donnywals.com. @Entry @property macro generates all conformance boilerplate; EnvironmentValues becomes type-safe and zero-boilerplate.
keyFindings.implication: v2 framework should categorize tokens: (1) scalar constants (DS.Spacing, DS.Radius) → static let in enum; (2) cascading values (theme, locale, accessibility) → @Entry in EnvironmentValues; (3) semantic colors → Asset Catalog + Color extension. Drift signal: direct environment(...) calls with non-semantic values; raw hardcoded theme switching without EnvironmentKey.

keyFindings.insight: JSON manifest (design-system.json) should record: token name, value(s), category (spacing/color/typography/component), codegen source (Asset Catalog path, Swift file location, SwiftTokenGen input), decision-log entry if intentional exception. This becomes the single source of truth for scoring and reporting drift.
keyFindings.evidence: Design System Consistency Framework (manifest structure), designsystemscollective.com (Tokens to Code Chapter 2). Manifest enables Mode B retrieval ("does this token exist?") and Mode A reporting ("which values are off-scale?"). DTCG JSON format is cross-platform standard.
keyFindings.implication: v2 should generate manifest from codegen output (SwiftTokenGen input JSON + discovered tokens via grep). Manifest structure: { tokens: [ { name: 'spacing.md', value: 16, category: 'spacing', source: 'DS.swift:48', codegen: true }, ... ], exceptions: [ { name: 'customSpacing', value: 19, reason: 'legacy modal constraint' } ], lastAudit: '2025-06-02' }. Scorer compares live code against manifest.

keyFindings.insight: Fragments (usefragments.com) is an emerging tool for design-system drift detection in CI/CD. design-extract tool supports DTCG tokens, multi-platform codegen (iOS/Android/Flutter), and CSS health audit. Both tools suggest that integrated AI-driven design-consistency checking is becoming standard practice.
keyFindings.evidence: usefragments.com (UI Governance for Design Systems), github.com/Manavarya09/design-extract (Extract website design systems). Fragments detects component mismatches and token drift pre-commit; design-extract supports multi-platform codegen from website inspection.
keyFindings.implication: v3 scorer should evolve toward Fragments-style integration: visual diff + token audit in CI. v2 should establish baseline metrics (number of violations by category, token reuse %, off-scale exceptions). Design-extract's multi-platform codegen approach suggests future: single JSON source → iOS SwiftUI, Android Compose, Flutter—v2 manifest format should be cross-platform compatible.

recommendationsForFramework: Expand v1 to explicitly model @Entry-based Environment tokens: introduce EnvironmentToken category in manifest and provide @Entry boilerplate template. Show how theme injection cascades to leaf views without prop-drilling.

Add Asset Catalog strategy to v1: document the light/dark ColorSet structure, show how to extend Color with semantic names, and explain why Asset Catalog is ergonomic (zero code, automatic dark mode). Provide XCAssets folder scaffold + color naming conventions.

Define JSON→Swift codegen workflow: v2 manifest should be DTCG-compatible (or Style Dictionary format). Show build-step integration (SwiftTokenGen or custom script) to generate DS enum from JSON. Codegen source code should be gitignored; manifest is the source of truth.

Codify SwiftLint enforcement configuration: v2 should include a .swiftlint.yml template with no_magic_numbers enabled + custom_rules banning Color.red, bare padding/frame/cornerRadius, inline .font(.system(size:)). Rules should be configurable per project (whitelist exceptions with // swiftlint:disable). CI should fail on violations.

Build static-analysis grep library: v2 scorer baseline should include curated patterns for drift signals (spacing literals, color abuse, font definitions, modifier chains). Patterns should be testable + documented. Advanced scorer (v3) should add SourceKit AST analysis to detect unregistered constants and trace value origins.

Establish manifest schema and auto-discovery: v2 should define design-system.json schema (DTCG subset). Scorer should auto-populate manifest by (1) parsing SwiftTokenGen output, (2) running grep patterns to detect live tokens, (3) comparing against expected tokens. Manifest becomes queryable ("which colors exist?", "off-scale spacing values?").

Model token categories explicitly: v2 framework should categorize tokens as (1) scalar constants (enum statics), (2) cascading values (@Entry Environment), (3) semantic colors (Asset Catalog), (4) components (Style protocols + ViewModifiers), (5) layouts (custom Layout protocol). Each category has different enforcement rules and codegen strategy.

Introduce ShapeStyle-based color pattern: v2 should show how to extend ShapeStyle where Self == Color to create design tokens that work in foregroundStyle(), fill(), stroke() without casting. This is more ergonomic than separate Color extensions and enables single-API color system.

Add custom Layout enforcement pattern: v2 should provide DSSpacingVStack/HStack examples that accept only enum-based spacing (not CGFloat), making raw-literal spacing detectable as anti-pattern. Show how Layout.placeSubviews() respects Subview.spacing(from:) to enforce platform rules.

Create decision-log template: v2 should formalize intentional exceptions (off-scale values, hardcoded strings, deprecated tokens). Decision log should be part of manifest and queryable by scorer. Prevents future audits from "fixing" deliberate deviations.

Define drift-reporting format: v2 scorer should report violations as (1) category (spacing, color, typography, component), (2) count (4 distinct button heights), (3) locations (file:line), (4) suggested fixes (snap to nearest DS token). Report should be human-readable + machine-parseable (JSON) for CI integration.

Plan v3 evolution toward multi-platform: manifest and codegen should be designed so iOS SwiftUI, Android Compose, and Flutter can share token definitions. Design-extract and style-dictionary patterns suggest future where single JSON source drives all platforms. v2 should not lock into iOS-only assumptions.
pitfalls: Believing @Entry eliminates the need for scalar constant enums: @Entry is for cascading values (theme, density), not spacing/sizing primitives. DS.Spacing should still be an enum of static constants, not Environment values—Environment has runtime cost and is overkill for layout constants. Misuse leads to poor ergonomics (always reaching into Environment for DS.Spacing.md).

Assuming Asset Catalog colors eliminate the need for semantic extensions: Asset Catalog provides dark-mode support and centralization, but semantic naming (Color.dsSurface instead of Color("Surface")) is orthogonal and essential. Raw Color("Surface") loses intent; developers don't know why Surface matters. Both are needed.

Treating Style protocols as optional: many projects define one ButtonStyle and expect developers to reuse it. In practice, if it's not the default or highly ergonomic, developers create inline custom styles. Enforce by (1) making default styles apply globally, (2) providing no-argument convenience views (DSButton, DSCard) that wrap Style, (3) linting against custom button construction patterns.

Overlooking custom Layout as an enforcement tool: Layout protocol is powerful for enforcing spacing rules structurally, but it's underused. Developers often use VStack + padding instead of custom layout, which bypasses spacing validation. Promote DSSpacingVStack as the preferred construct for common patterns.

Assuming grep patterns are sufficient for drift detection: grep catches obvious violations (Color.red, padding(16)) but misses subtle drift (padding(DS.Spacing.md + 1), using Designer-approved hardcoded value documented in decision log). AST analysis via SourceKit can trace constant origins and flag unregistered values. Grep is necessary but not sufficient.

Generating manifest without codegen integration: if the manifest is manually maintained while code is generated (or vice versa), they diverge. Establish a CI check that codegen output matches manifest, and that live code matches both. Consider manifest as derived, not source—source is JSON tokens or AST analysis of live code.

Failing to make @Entry and ViewModifier patterns clear: developers often confuse when to use EnvironmentKey (cascading values) vs. ViewModifier (styling) vs. Style protocol (controls). A well-written pattern library should show decision trees and examples for each. Vague guidance leads to misuse.

Underestimating the friction of onboarding new tokens: every new token requires (1) JSON entry, (2) codegen run, (3) manifest update, (4) code change, (5) Asset Catalog entry if color. If the workflow is not automated (single-command build step), developers will create bare values to avoid friction. Automate aggressively.

Not documenting intentional exceptions visibly: if off-scale values exist (e.g., modal-specific spacing), they should be adjacent to the code with a clear reason (linked to decision-log entry). Otherwise, audits treat them as drift and "fix" them silently. Decision log must be part of CI checks and reporting.

Assuming developers will write Style protocols: many developers prefer modifiers or inline styling because it feels more direct. Style protocols require more boilerplate (Configuration struct, makeBody method). Reduce friction by providing templates/macros (Swift 5.9+) and examples. Default should be Style protocol; modifiers are fallback.

Treating design-system.json as a design tool instead of an engineering artifact: if designers control the JSON directly (via Figma export or tool), and engineers must parse it, mismatches happen. Instead, JSON should be either (1) engineer-owned (built from live code audit), (2) auto-generated from Figma (via figma-tokens, design-extract), or (3) version-controlled and reviewed like code.

Overlooking dark mode in static analysis: drift detection should account for dark-mode variants (Color named correctly for dark, but Asset Catalog appearance not set). Scorer should check that all semantic colors have both light and dark variants in Asset Catalog, not just that they're named correctly.

facets.facet: Agent-Driven Design System Convergence Framework: Behavioral Protocols & Manifest-Presentation Design

keyFindings.insight: Multi-agent convergence requires a **retrieve-before-create enforcement protocol** that operationalizes as a mandatory decision tree: (1) read canonical manifest, (2) semantic intent matching against catalog, (3) similarity threshold gate (0.75–0.85 for high-confidence reuse), (4) snap to nearest token if match found, (5) only then create, (6) auto-register to prevent orphans. Without structural enforcement (linting gates, manifest-read attestation), agents revert to invention.
keyFindings.evidence: ARCS framework (synthesize-execute-repair loop) and RepoAI multi-agent orchestration show that RAG systems with explicit retrieve-before-generate phases reduce hallucination and accelerate convergence. Memento-Skills system uses persistent structured markdown skills (external memory) as the agent's evolving knowledge base. Agentic memory systems (G-Memory, MemAdapter) demonstrate that hierarchical, multi-level graph structures coordinate cross-agent knowledge via selective sharing controllers.
keyFindings.implication: The framework must hardcode retrieval as a precondition to creation, not a courtesy check.
